newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russian Tyumen oil big on reserves, problems.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russian Tyumen oil big on reserves, problems.

text.p: Everything about Russia's Tyumen Oil Company is big, from its reserves to its battles with subsidaries, making the latest energy firm to be sold off a measure of the woes of Russia's oil sector.

Officials at Tyumen Oil, known as TNK, urged the company's main subsidiary on Thursday to come back to the fold and support TNK's privatisation, saying big money was needed to reinvigorate its giant Samotlor oilfield.
But officials and energy analysts alike said TNK embodied the worst of the management rows and financial chaos plaguing Russian oil firms, and they said its future would be tough.

"For us, it's clear that without finances, we cannot develop further or find serious partners and investors," said TNK board chairman Nikolai Rusanov, referring to an ongoing investment tender for 40 percent of the company.
"It's important the winner have resources of $6 or $7 billion to reconstruct Samotlor and tap new reserves," he said.
That is hardly likely, analysts said, given the tender is closed to Russian banks and foreign investors.
TNK's future depends on the giant but declining West Siberian field for which it holds a development licence.

"The company's not an inherent loser, but it's a loser right now," said energy analyst Peter Houlder, managing director of CentreInvest Securities in Moscow. "Restructuring could be done, but it will be extremely tough."

Other analysts agreed, citing TNK's major row with its subsidiary and main oil production unit Nizhnevartovskneftegaz over who should win the privatisation process and take charge of the company's fate.
"It doesn't seem to be a very promising company," Renaissance Capital analyst Alexei Kokin said. "In spite of its reserves, its production costs are prohibitively high."
TNK's 1996 production, some seven percent of total oil output in Russia, the world's third largest oil producer, slipped six percent to 426,000 barrels per day.
The company's one refinery, in Ryazan, had such troubles with feedstock supplies that it processed only half the planned total last year. Operations are forecast to contract this year.
Nizhnevartovskneftegaz owed the government budget 1.1 trillion roubles ($190 million) as of June and has its own problems -- it is one of the few companies the state says it may actually bankrupt.
Nizhnevartovskneftegaz's managing director, Viktor Pali, has sparred with TNK managers over privatisation, in battles typical of the byzantine quarrels between managers at Russian oil firms.
A TNK press release said TNK would hold an emergency shareholders' meeting on August 2 to elect a new board, decide whether to sack Pali, and to change TNK's charter.

The moves could give former Fuel and Energy Minister Yuri Shafranik, the former TNK board chairman, a formal job at the company after what TNK called a paperwork error kept him off the ballot at the annual meeting earlier this month.
Moscow, in one of the last stages of its oil sector privatisation programme, is selling a 40 percent state stake in TNK through an investment tender closing July 16.
It will offer approximately 49 percent at a separate cash auction in August.

Rusanov said Russia's Alfa-Group, which includes commodities powerhouse Alfa-Ekho, and Rosneftinvest, an unknown entity allied with Nizhnevartovskneftegaz, were both interested in acquiring the 40 percent stake.
The sales are designed to raise cash for TNK, which is nearly 91 percent state owned and one of the last vertically integrated oil firms to be created.
But instead they are raising hackles.
"The longterm investor able to spend or raise billions of dollars to rehabilitate Samotlor does not exist in Russia right now," Kokin said.
Samotlor has yielded 2.2 billion tonnes of oil since it opened in the 1960s and still has 1.5 billion left.
TNK President Alexander Furman told a news conference TNK was in talks with Tyumen regional authorities over how they could acquire most of the 49 percent stake.
But Furman, appointed only this week, pleaded for time to get to know his new company when queried about his strategy for moving TNK into the future.
"I only just got here," he said. "Just please give me two weeks and then we'll talk again."
